hints: The null hypothesis is that the machine is fair: $\text{P}(0) = \dfrac{1}{10}$. Bob suspects the probability is **smaller**, so choose the direction of $\text{H}_1$ from that.
walkthrough:
**Hypotheses**

$\text{H}_0$ is the 'nothing unusual' statement. A fair machine produces each digit with equal probability, so the digit $0$ comes up with probability $\dfrac{1}{10}$.

Bob thinks the probability is **less than** $\dfrac{1}{10}$, so $\text{H}_1$ uses $<$ (one-tailed, lower tail).

$$\text{H}_0: \text{P}(0) = \frac{1}{10} \qquad \text{H}_1: \text{P}(0) < \frac{1}{10}$$

**Final answer**

$\text{H}_0: p = \dfrac{1}{10}$ and $\text{H}_1: p < \dfrac{1}{10}$, where $p$ is the probability that the machine produces the digit $0$.

hints: Under $\text{H}_0$ the number of zeros $X$ in $30$ digits is Binomial: $X \sim \text{B}(30, 0.1)$. You must use this distribution, not merely write it.
The rejection region is in the lower tail. Start with the smallest value: $\text{P}(X = 0) = 0.9^{30}$. Is it at most the $10\%$ significance level?
Now check the next value: $\text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = 0.9^{30} + 30 \times 0.9^{29} \times 0.1$. Is it still at most $0.1$?
The rejection region is the largest set of values $\{0, 1, \ldots\}$ whose total probability does not go above $0.1$. Decide where to stop, using your two comparisons.
walkthrough:
**What a rejection region is**

The rejection region is the set of results so low that, if $\text{H}_0$ were true, they would have a probability of $10\%$ or less. If Bob's count falls in it, he rejects $\text{H}_0$. Because $\text{H}_1$ is $p < \frac{1}{10}$, the region is at the **lower** end: $X \leqslant c$ for some $c$.

**The distribution under $\text{H}_0$ (the first M1 mark)**

There are $30$ digits, each one is a $0$ or not independently, so with $p = 0.1$:

$$X \sim \text{B}(30, 0.1)$$

where $X$ is the number of zeros in the $30$ digits. The mark is for **using** it in the working below.

**Test $X = 0$ (the second M1 mark)**

$X = 0$ means all $30$ digits are non-zeros. Each has probability $0.9$:

$$\text{P}(X = 0) = 0.9^{30} = 0.0424$$

$0.0424 < 0.1$, so $X = 0$ is in the rejection region.

**Test $X \leqslant 1$ (the B1 mark)**

$X \leqslant 1$ means $X = 0$ or $X = 1$. For $X = 1$ choose which one of the $30$ digits is the zero: $30$ ways.

$$\text{P}(X = 1) = 30 \times 0.9^{29} \times 0.1 = 0.1413$$

$$\text{P}(X \leqslant 1) = 0.0424 + 0.1413 = 0.184$$

(Using more decimal places: $0.042391 + 0.141304 = 0.183695$. The scheme accepts $0.184$ or $0.183$.)

$0.184 > 0.1$, so $X = 1$ is **not** in the rejection region. Adding it would push the probability over $10\%$.

**State the rejection region (the A1 mark)**

$X = 0$ is in, $X \leqslant 1$ is out. So the only value in the rejection region is $0$.

Note: this mark needs at least one comparison with $0.1$ shown.

**Final answer**

The rejection region is $X = 0$, that is, $0$ zeros in the $30$ digits.

hints: A Type I error means rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is true. Find the probability of landing in your rejection region when $p = \dfrac{1}{10}$. You have already worked this out in **(b)**.
walkthrough:
**What a Type I error is**

A Type I error happens when we **reject** $\text{H}_0$ even though $\text{H}_0$ is **true**. The probability of this is the probability of landing in the rejection region when $p = \frac{1}{10}$.

The rejection region from **(b)** is just $X = 0$, and we found $\text{P}(X = 0) = 0.9^{30}$.

**Final answer**

$\text{P}(\text{Type I error}) = 0.0424$ (3 significant figures). Note that it is less than the $10\%$ significance level, because the distribution is discrete and the next value would have taken us over $10\%$.

hints: Now the true probability of a zero is $\dfrac{1}{40}$, so the number of zeros in $30$ digits is $\text{B}(30, \dfrac{1}{40})$.

A Type II error means **not** rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is false, i.e. $X$ lands **outside** your rejection region. Use the complement: $1 - \text{P}(X = 0)$, where $\text{P}(X = 0) = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{40}\right)^{30}$.
Work out $1 - \dfrac{1}{40}$ first, raise it to the power $30$ on the calculator, and subtract the result from $1$.
walkthrough:
**The true distribution (the B1 mark)**

The machine actually produces a $0$ once in every $40$ digits, so the real probability of a $0$ is $\dfrac{1}{40} = 0.025$. For the $30$ digits,

$$X \sim \text{B}\left(30, \frac{1}{40}\right)$$

**What a Type II error is**

A Type II error means we **fail to reject** $\text{H}_0$ when it is actually false (here it is false, since $\frac{1}{40} < \frac{1}{10}$). We fail to reject when $X$ is **not** in the rejection region $\{0\}$, that is, $X \geqslant 1$.

$$\text{P}(\text{Type II error}) = \text{P}(X \geqslant 1) = 1 - \text{P}(X = 0)$$

**Calculate (the M1 and A1 marks)**

$\text{P}(X = 0)$ means every digit is non-zero. The chance of a non-zero digit is $1 - \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{39}{40} = 0.975$.

$$\text{P}(X = 0) = 0.975^{30} = 0.4679$$

$$1 - 0.975^{30} = 1 - 0.4679 = 0.5321$$

(Using more decimal places: $1 - 0.467884 = 0.532116$.)

hints: A Type II error means $\text{H}_0$ is not rejected although it is false. Put that into the words of this question (the machine, the digit $0$, Bob's conclusion).
walkthrough:
**Translate the definition into this context**

Generally, a Type II error is: **not rejecting** $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is **false**.

Here, $\text{H}_0$ says the probability of a $0$ is $\dfrac{1}{10}$. It is false when the probability really is less than $\dfrac{1}{10}$. Not rejecting means Bob does not conclude that the probability is lower.

**Final answer**

A Type II error means Bob concludes there is no evidence that the probability of the machine producing a $0$ is less than $\dfrac{1}{10}$ (he does not reject $\text{H}_0$), when in fact the probability **is** less than $\dfrac{1}{10}$.
